Research task (web + academic literature, use WebSearch/WebFetch extensively, 2023–2026 papers, blogs, GitHub). Do NOT modify any files.

Context: we build an LLM agent (Claude Sonnet via the Claude Code CLI, tools via MCP, Playwright browser over CDP) that must, within 20 minutes, navigate 4 unfamiliar enterprise-like websites (tender portal, supplier spec portal, SAP-style ERP with transaction codes and F4 search popups, webmail with paging/archive), extract ~100 facts (quantities, revisions, prices with scales/validity, approvals, emails), then fill and sign a multi-step web form. The final evaluation runs on UNSEEN websites (different software/layout/navigation), so the approach must be fully general (no site-specific selectors or URL patterns in code). Rules forbid a crawler that autonomously discovers everything; a model must choose navigation, but helpers may extract a selected page, paginate a model-selected result set, fill forms, calculate. Ranking: correctness first (must be 100%), then cost × time. Current state: 100% achieved, ~250-400 s, ~$1.2 (dominated by cache-read tokens: ~55 turns × large context) and ~70 s spent generating a 12k-token final JSON.

Find GENUINELY USEFUL, concrete, evidence-backed techniques for:
1. Cutting agent cost/latency: observation masking vs summarization (e.g., JetBrains "The Complexity Trap" 2025), context offloading to filesystem (Manus context engineering), tool-result clearing, parallel tool calls, batching, fewer turns, speculative actions, smaller observation formats (accessibility tree vs DOM vs markdown; e.g., Agent-E DOM distillation, "Beyond Browsing: API-based web agents" Song et al. 2024 hybrid API+browse; network/XHR interception to call JSON endpoints directly).
2. Reliability/accuracy of extraction: verbatim-quote grounding / attribution verification, self-consistency across runs, verifier agents, structured outputs, per-field confidence.
3. Web form filling robustness on unseen forms (multi-step wizards, modals, TAN/2FA): best practices from WebArena/VisualWebArena/WorkArena/Mind2Web SOTA agents (e.g., Agent S, Browser Use, OpenAI Operator/CUA, Anthropic computer use, AgentOccam, "SteP", Jace, Surfer-H), and what simplifications of the observation/action space gave the biggest gains (AgentOccam showed simplifying observation/action space gave big gains).
4. Multi-agent orchestration patterns that actually helped (planner/executor, per-site subagents, Anthropic's multi-agent research system blog).
5. Output-token latency: ways to avoid emitting large JSON at the end (incremental recording tools, compact formats).

For each technique: one-paragraph summary, source URL, the measured effect reported, and a concrete idea for how it applies to our setup with an estimated benefit. Rank by expected impact for our setting. Be concrete and skeptical; flag hype. Final report under 1500 words.

"The Complexity Trap" is a 2025 paper from JetBrains Research and the Technical University of Munich (Tobias Lindenbauer, Igor Slinko, Ludwig Felder, Egor Bogomolov, Yaroslav Zharov). It asks whether the more complex LLM summarization used in agent context management actually beats a simpler approach.

**Problem:** Agent context grows with every tool call. A single action can yield thousands of tokens, whether from reading an entire source file, running a recursive directory listing, or a lengthy test suite log. The paper reports that observation tokens make up around 84% of an average SWE-agent turn in its preliminary experiments.

**Approaches compared:** Observation masking drops or hides older tool outputs, while LLM summarization asks a model to condense older parts of the trajectory. OpenHands or Cursor use summarization, and the authors note that the key difference is whether they discard or condense old context.

**Findings:** The experiments ran within SWE-agent on SWE-bench Verified across five model configurations. The authors found that a simple environment observation masking strategy halves cost relative to the raw agent while matching, and sometimes slightly exceeding, the solve rate of LLM summarization. In one example, masking raised the solve rate for Qwen3-Coder 480B from 53.8% to 54.8%. They also introduced a hybrid approach that further reduces costs by 7% and 11% compared to just observation masking or LLM summarization, respectively. The authors say they raise concerns regarding the trend towards pure LLM summarization, and they note initial evidence that the findings generalize to the OpenHands scaffold.

**Resources:** The code and data are on GitHub and Hugging Face under the JetBrains-Research organization. The paper was published as an arXiv preprint (2508.21433) and presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop on deep learning for code.

Manus's own write-up and secondary summaries cover the KV-cache lessons well. The search results say less about the file-system approach, so that part is thinner.

**KV-cache as the core metric**
Manus treats KV-cache hit rate as the main production metric. The reasoning is economic: their agents process roughly 100 input tokens for every output token, so reusing cached prefixes cuts both latency and cost. With Claude Sonnet, cached input tokens cost 0.30 USD/MTok, while uncached ones cost 3 USD/MTok—a 10x difference.

**Practices for keeping the cache warm**
- **Stable prefixes.** Because of how autoregressive models work, even a single-token difference can invalidate the cache from that token onward. A common culprit is a timestamp at the top of the system prompt.

6. **Keep errors in context:** Leave failed actions, observations, and stack traces visible rather than cleaning them up. The model updates its beliefs and is less likely to repeat the mistake. The authors treat error recovery as a key sign of agentic behavior.

Prune4Web is a 2025 paper from Beihang University (Zhang et al.) that tackles the problem of feeding huge DOM trees to LLM web agents. Its core idea is to have the model write executable Python that prunes the DOM, rather than having the LLM filter it directly.

- **Filtering:** A rule-based pass first keeps elements with clear interactive features, such as links, buttons, inputs, or certain role attributes. - **Action grounding:** An LLM-based grounder selects the specific action from the pruned candidates.

**Results:** The authors report that the approach achieves a 25x to 50x reduction in candidate elements for grounding. On low-level sub-task grounding, accuracy rose from 46.80% to 88.28%. **Subagent output to a filesystem**
- Subagents save their work to external storage and send only lightweight references back to the coordinator. This avoids losing information across stages and cuts the token cost of copying large outputs through the conversation.
- The article notes this works best for structured outputs like code, reports, or data visualizations.

**Tool description improvements**
- The team built a tool-testing agent that tried flawed MCP tools dozens of times and rewrote their descriptions.
- Future agents using the new descriptions finished tasks 40% faster, because they made fewer mistakes.

**Tasks where multi-agent systems are a poor fit**
- Domains where all agents must share the same context.
- Tasks with many dependencies between agents.
- Most coding tasks, which have fewer parallelizable parts than research.
- Tasks whose value is too low to justify the cost. Multi-agent systems use about 15× the tokens of chat interactions.

**End-state evaluation**
- For agents that change persistent state over many turns, judge whether the agent reached the correct final state rather than whether it followed a prescribed process.
- For complex workflows, split evaluation into checkpoints where specific state changes should have happened.

**LLM-as-judge**
- A rubric scores outputs on factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.
- The team found that one LLM call with one prompt, returning a 0.0-1.0 score and a pass/fail grade, was the most consistent and matched human judgments best.

LangExtract's grounding is a documented core feature. Its span-to-source mapping is useful, but it only verifies against the text it was given, and the verification step is manual or at least not built in.

**How grounding works**
- The library records where each extraction sits in the input. One description says it maps each extracted item back to the original text by recording character offsets or spans. Google's own announcement says that every extracted entity is mapped back to its exact character offsets in the source text.
- The offsets refer to the original document even when it is chunked. A third-party Elixir port documents this, noting that chunk-relative positions are adjusted before spans are returned. That port is not Google's Python library, so its details may differ from the original.
- Its spans also come with an alignment status. The Elixir port reports `:exact`, `:lesser`, `:fuzzy`, or `:not_found`, which signals how confidently each extraction matched the source. I could not confirm whether the official Python package uses the same labels.

**Verification**
- The main built-in check is visual. Google says the approach visually highlights each extraction in the original text, making it much easier to evaluate and verify the extracted information. A review analysis notes that it ships an interactive HTML visualization (`lx.visualize()`) that highlights each extraction in the source text, which is genuinely useful for spot-checking grounding by eye during development.
- Grounding does not confirm correctness. The same analysis points out that LangExtract grounds to a character offset in text, which presumes the text is already correct — so on a scanned document, the grounding is only as good as whatever OCR ran upstream, and a confidently cited value can still be wrong.
- The library does not measure accuracy. The same source states that neither LangExtract nor LlamaExtract appears in any public document extraction benchmark, so you would need your own labeled test set to measure accuracy.

**Caveats**
- Maturity: one vendor page says not an officially supported Google product. Google's documentation states users must acknowledge LangExtract's experimental status when deploying in production or citing it in publications. I could not verify the official documentation directly, so check it before relying on this.
- Compliance claims: one site says the grounding supports HIPAA audit trail requirements by maintaining character-level traceability for every extracted entity. Treat that as a vendor's marketing claim, not a compliance determination.
- Version: a directory lists v1.6.0 (2026-07-02) as the latest release. I did not check the GitHub repository directly.

Practical takeaway: use the offsets to link each extraction to its source, then run the HTML visualization or a script that checks `text[start:end]` against the extracted value. Then sample documents for human review, especially scanned ones. If you use the Elixir port, note that its offsets are in bytes rather than characters, so slicing by character count will return the wrong text.

content.text:
I've ranked the techniques below by expected impact on your setup. Every number comes from the cited source; anything I couldn't confirm is marked. One piece of arithmetic drives most of the ranking: Sonnet cache reads cost $0.30/MTok, so your ~$1.2 is roughly 3–4M cache-read tokens (about 55 turns × 60k average context). Cost grows with turns × context size, so the biggest wins come from making context smaller where it's born and from splitting it up. Trimming wording helps much less.

## 1. Keep tool results small from the start, with a handle to fetch the full page again (highest impact)

**Summary.** Manus drops bulky page or document content from context but keeps a URL or file path so it can be fetched again ("restorable compression"). It treats the file system as memory and the KV-cache hit rate as its main production metric. Its input:output ratio is about 100:1, and cached Sonnet input is 10× cheaper. Browser Use's `extract` tool runs a separate call over the page markdown and returns only the answer instead of loading 20k+ token pages into the agent's context. AgentOccam's observation simplification (removing redundant elements, Markdown restructuring) plus action-space pruning took WebArena from 16.5% (plain agent) to 43.1%. Its paper gives no clean per-component gain for observation alone; the per-step breakdown is only in a figure. Prune4Web pre-filters the DOM in code: 25–50× fewer candidate elements, and grounding accuracy went from 46.8% to 88.3%.

**Sources:** https://manus.im/blog/Context-Engineering-for-AI-Agents-Lessons-from-Building-Manus · https://browser-use.com/posts/speed-matters · https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13825 · https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/40772/44733

**Apply.** Each MCP page tool keeps the full page text on the server under a handle and returns only a compact outline: headings, interactive elements with short IDs, table headers with row counts, and the first N rows. Add `page_find(handle, query)` and `page_rows(handle, range)` so the model can pull specific spans. In the Claude Code CLI you can't remove a tool result after it's in history, so the result has to be small when it's first returned. **Estimate:** average context down 40–60%, cost down 35–50%. The model still chooses what to read, which stays within the fair-play rules.

## 2. One parallel subagent per site, writing results to files

**Summary.** Anthropic's research system has a lead agent plus 3–5 parallel subagents, each also calling tools in parallel. It reports up to 90% less research time and +90.2% on its internal eval versus a single agent. Subagents write their output to storage and pass back references, which avoids a "game of telephone" through the conversation. Token usage alone explained 80% of the performance variance on BrowseComp. The catch: about 15× the tokens of a chat, and a poor fit when tasks share context or depend heavily on each other.

**Source:** https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system

**Apply.** Because cost scales with turns × context, four subagents of about 14 turns each over separate small contexts cost much less in cache reads than one 55-turn context. Wall-clock time becomes roughly the slowest site instead of the sum of all four. A short planner turn first collects the cross-site keys (tender ID, material numbers) and hands them to each subagent. Each subagent adds about 10–20k tokens of startup context (third-party estimate, unverified), so keep subagent prompts lean. **Estimate:** 40–60% less time, 20–40% less cost. Risk: a fact that only shows up on another site (for example, an email that changes a quantity). Handle it with an explicit reconciliation step.

## 3. Stop generating the 12k-token final JSON

**Summary.** Browser Use measured output tokens at about 215× the time cost of input tokens (10 output tokens ≈ 62.6 ms; 1k input tokens ≈ 29.1 ms). They kept actions to 10–15 tokens. YAML or tabular formats save about 20–35% of tokens versus JSON. That comes from mixed-quality sources, and gains are small for short outputs.

**Sources:** https://browser-use.com/posts/speed-matters · https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.00887

**Apply, in order of payoff:**
- **(a) Record facts by pointer.** `record(field_path, handle, span_id)`: code copies the exact text from the stored page, normalizes numbers and dates, and builds the final JSON plus the form fill. The model emits a few tokens per fact, and each value is verbatim by construction.
- **(b) Record facts as they're found.** If you don't use pointers, record each fact during exploration so the output is spread across turns, or emitted concurrently by the subagents in #2.
- **(c) Compact keys and TSV** for whatever the model must still write.

**Estimate:** saves about 60 of the 70 seconds at the end. This also feeds the reliability work in #6.

## 4. Fewer turns: macro actions, parallel calls, better tool descriptions

**Summary.** When Anthropic rewrote its tool descriptions using an agent that tested the tools, later agents finished tasks 40% faster. AgentOccam and SteP show that higher-level actions and policies help: SteP raised WebArena from 14.9% to about 33–36% with 2.3× smaller context. One caution: in an Online-Mind2Web failure analysis, grounding errors were more likely when several actions ran before the next observation.

**Sources:** https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents · https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.03720 · https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.02031

**Apply:**
- `fill_fields({label: value, ...})` fills a whole step and returns a readback of what's actually in the fields.
- `paginate_extract(handle, max_pages)` covers model-selected result sets (allowed by your rules).
- Instruct the agent to issue independent reads in parallel within one turn.
- Batch actions only where you also read back the result.

**Estimate:** 20–35% fewer turns.

## 5. Use JSON from the site's own network calls when it's there

**Summary.** "Beyond Browsing" (CMU): browsing only 14.8%, API only 29.2%, hybrid 38.9% on WebArena (v3). The API advantage shrinks on sites with poor API support. WALT (Salesforce, ICLR 2026) turns UI flows into URL-parameter tools: 50.1% on WebArena and +20.5% over a tool-free baseline on Online-Mind2Web.

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.16464 · https://proceedings.iclr.cc/paper_files/paper/2026/hash/5b175f9e93873e3a10a6ce43dbb82e05-Abstract-Conference.html

**Apply.** Use a CDP listener that saves JSON/XHR responses for the page the model chose and lists them as another source the model can read. Also let the model edit query parameters (page size, filters) on URLs it has already seen. **Caveat:** SAP-style and webmail mockups are often server-rendered, so this may do nothing on the unseen sites. **Estimate:** large where it applies (one call instead of paging), zero otherwise. It's generic, so it's cheap insurance.

## 6. Reliability: checks in code first, a verifier model only for what code can't check

**Summary.**
- LangExtract maps each extracted value to exact character offsets in the source and reports exact or fuzzy alignment. It has no published accuracy benchmark.
- Surfer-H uses a separate validator. Swapping a weaker model in as validator dropped accuracy by 12–16 points, so validation needs a strong model.
- WorkArena checks results by querying the saved database, not the confirmation screen.
- ClawBench reports common failures: missing required fields, skipped confirmation steps, and mis-clicks on elements with similar labels (secondary summary).
- Self-consistency across runs: the evidence for extraction is weak and depends on the model, and a 2025 abstract argues it has become wasteful with stronger models.

**Sources:** https://developers.googleblog.com/en/introducing-langextract-a-gemini-powered-information-extraction-library/ · https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02865 · https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07718 · https://api.emergentmind.com/topics/clawbench

**Apply:**
- Every recorded value must match a substring of its source span. That comes free with #3a.
- Deterministic checks: totals add up, price-scale tiers are monotone, validity dates cover the bid date, revision is the latest.
- Before signing, compare the form against the record store field by field, and re-read the confirmation page.
- Spend extra model calls only on fields flagged as conflicting: two sources disagree, or there are multiple revisions or validity windows. Skip whole-run self-consistency; it roughly doubles cost for little gain at your accuracy level.

## 7. Masking old tool results (useful if you own the conversation loop)

**Summary.** "The Complexity Trap" (JetBrains, NeurIPS 2025 workshop) found that masking old observations with a rolling window of the last 10 roughly halved cost (−51% to −57% across models) with solve rates statistically unchanged. LLM summarization made trajectories longer (52 vs 44 turns) and its summary calls broke caching. The best window depended on the scaffold (10 for SWE-agent, 58 for OpenHands). Anthropic's context editing cut tokens 84% on a 100-turn search eval.

**Sources:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21433 · https://claude.com/blog/context-management

**Caveat for you.** With Anthropic caching, every mask invalidates the cached prefix and rewrites the remainder at 1.25×, which is why the API has a `clear_at_least` threshold. I didn't confirm whether the CLI exposes context editing; in practice it only gets auto-compaction. If you move to your own loop, mask in large batches. Otherwise #1 gets you most of this benefit. Never use LLM summarization here.

## 8. Low priority or overstated

- **Speculative actions** (ICLR 2026 oral): at most 20% lower latency at 55% next-action prediction accuracy, and it costs extra branches. Skip it. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04371
- **Code execution / programmatic tool calling:** Anthropic's 98.7% figure is one worked example; the 37% figure (complex research tasks) comes from secondary sources and I couldn't find it on Anthropic's page. It would only help if the model scripted multi-page reads, which risks the "crawler" rule. https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/code-execution-with-mcp
- **Benchmark scores generally:** "An Illusion of Progress" (COLM 2025) found most agents' self-reported WebVoyager scores, including Browser Use and Agent-E-style setups, fall to about 30% under human evaluation on Online-Mind2Web, with Operator at about 61%. Don't copy architectures because of leaderboard numbers. https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.01382
- **Screenshots** helped GPT-4o only very slightly on WorkArena and add about 0.8 s per step in Browser Use. Use the accessibility tree or distilled DOM, with screenshots only when visuals matter.

## Suggested order

Doing #1, #3a and #2 together should get you to roughly $0.4–0.6 and about 150–200 s. These are my estimates, not measured. Add #6's code checks so you stay at 100%. #4 is quick tuning work, and #5 is opportunistic.
